Booker T. Washington. The educator and racial leader whose vision of vocational training and economic self-sufficiency shaped Black institutions throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. He founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881, and it became one of the most prestigious historically Black colleges and a major center for industrial education. In 1895 he delivered the Atlanta Compromise speech, calling for Black acceptance of social segregation in exchange for economic opportunity and white investment in Black education. This strategy gave him enormous influence among white philanthropists and politicians, who came to see him as the de facto Black mediator between the races. He advocated for economic self-help and vocational training over immediate demands for political equality, a philosophy he summarized as pulling yourself up by your bootstraps. He published his autobiography Up from Slavery in 1901, and it became a bestseller that shaped the narrative of the self-made man in American culture. Yet his accommodationist approach to Jim Crow segregation made him deeply controversial. W.E.B. Du Bois and younger intellectuals fiercely critiqued him, seeing his strategy as a betrayal of full citizenship rights. Malcolm X would later echo Washington's emphasis on Black economic independence, though without accommodating segregation. And while Martin Luther King Jr.'s successor movement would reject Washington's strategy entirely, it built upon the institutional foundation Tuskegee had established.
